data.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
data.summary:
Input: A list of integers nums that was originally sorted in ascending order and then rotated between 1 and n times.
Output: The minimum element in the array.
Rules: The algorithm must run in O(log n) time complexity.
constraints: All elements of nums are unique
nums is sorted and rotated between 1 and n times

data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    import random
    nums = list(range(n))
    k = rng.randint(0, n - 1)
    rotated = nums[k:] + nums[:k]
    return [rotated]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    import random
    nums = list(range(n))
    return [nums]

data.key_insight: In a rotated sorted array, one half of the array will always be sorted. We can compare the middle element with the rightmost element to determine which half is sorted and where the minimum element must reside.

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.detail: Set left pointer to 0 and right pointer to nums.length - 1.

steps.title: Binary search loop
steps.detail: While left is less than right, calculate the middle index. Compare nums[mid] with nums[right].

steps.title: Narrow search space
steps.detail: If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum element must be in the right half, so set left = mid + 1. Otherwise, the minimum is in the left half including mid, so set right = mid.

steps.title: Return result
steps.detail: When left equals right, the pointers converge on the minimum element, which is returned.

data.pattern_summary: Binary Search cuts the search space in half at each step by leveraging ordering properties, moving from O(n) to O(log n).

pattern_options.name: Binary Search
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The requirement for O(log n) time complexity directly points to halving the search space on each iteration.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers usually scan linearly or inward from both ends, which results in O(n) time for this problem.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Sliding window is used for contiguous sublists of a fixed or variable size, not for finding a global minimum in a rotated array.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: A hash map would require O(n) time to build and does not utilize the sorted and rotated property of the input.

signals.hint: Implies a structured order exists that we can exploit instead of checking every element.

signals.phrase: run in O(log n) time complexity
signals.hint: This is a strict performance requirement that forces logarithmic operations like halving the search space.

data.brute_force_idea: Iterate through every element in the list, keeping track of the smallest value seen so far.
data.brute_force_why: The loop visits each element in the list exactly once.
data.bottleneck: Checking every single element sequentially ignores the structural information provided by the sorted and rotated nature of the array.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many elements you examine in the worst case.
Ask yourself if you really need to inspect every element to find the minimum.
Think about how you can discard half of the elements immediately.

data.overview: This algorithm uses binary search to find the minimum element in a rotated sorted array in O(log n) time. By comparing the middle element with the rightmost element, it identifies which half of the array is unsorted and restricts the search space accordingly.
data.intuition: Imagine a mountain road that drops down into a valley and wraps around. If you look at the middle of your current path and see that it is higher than the far right end, you know the drop into the valley must be to your right.

flow_nodes.label: Initialize Pointers
flow_nodes.detail: Set left to 0 and right to len(nums) - 1.

flow_nodes.label: While left < right
flow_nodes.detail: Continue searching as long as left pointer is less than right pointer.

flow_nodes.label: Calculate mid
flow_nodes.detail: Find the middle index between left and right.

flow_nodes.label: nums[mid] > nums[right]?
flow_nodes.detail: Check if the middle element is greater than the rightmost element.

flow_nodes.label: left = mid + 1
flow_nodes.detail: Minimum must be in the right half.

flow_nodes.label: right = mid
flow_nodes.detail: Minimum must be in the left half including mid.

flow_nodes.label: Return nums[left]
flow_nodes.detail: When left equals right, we found the minimum element.

pitfalls: Using left <= right which can lead to an infinite loop when pointers converge.
Comparing nums[mid] with nums[left] instead of nums[right], which fails for certain rotated configurations.
Updating right to mid - 1, which might skip the actual minimum element if it happens to be at mid.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force solution scans every element, resulting in linear time. The optimized approach uses binary search to repeatedly cut the search space in half by comparing the middle element to the rightmost element to determine which half contains the pivot and the minimum value.

derivation.note: Pointers left and right are initialized once.
The while loop runs log n times as the search range is halved each iteration.
Midpoint calculation runs once per loop iteration.
Comparison runs once per loop iteration.
Pointer update runs once per loop iteration.
Result is returned once the loop terminates.

data.time_summary: Summing the costs of the lines, the while loop dominates execution. The measured evidence confirms this: when n doubles from 4 to 32, the total steps for the optimized solution grow slowly from 11 to 23, matching O(log n) scaling.
data.space_summary: Only a few scalar variables (left, right, mid) are stored, so memory usage is constant at O(1) extra space.
data.takeaway: When searching for a boundary or extreme value in a partially ordered or rotated array, use binary search by comparing against an endpoint to eliminate half the data each step.
mistakes: Using left <= right instead of left < right, which can cause an infinite loop when the pointers converge.
Comparing nums[mid] to nums[left] instead of nums[right], which breaks the logic because the minimum always lies in the unsorted half relative to the right pointer.
Updating right to mid - 1 instead of right = mid, which risks skipping over the actual minimum element.
